cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Hello, Fernley sports center. How can I help you?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Yes, I'd like to apply for one of the lifeguard jobs you advertise this week.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Right, we can do that now over the phone. I'll just need some information from you. Let me get a form.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Okay, so let's start with your name. Peter Smith.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay, can you let me have your home address?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: It's 130 South Main Street, Lake Elsonore.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay, I'm new around here. Can you spell that for me?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Yes, it's E-L-S-I-N-O-R-E. Q1

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay, got that. And your phone number?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: My home numbers 951-674-3124. Q9

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: But it's best to ring me on my cell phone. That's 0778-96245. Q2

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Now, what do you do? Are you still in college or are you working full time? I'm in my second year here at Fernley and this vacation I've got a job as a part-time waiter. Q3

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay, I guess if you're at Fernley College, you'll be studying physical education.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: And they all seem to do that there. That's right. Then I hope to go on and coach baseball in high school. Something like that. Q4

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: I guess it all depends on how I do in my final exams.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Okay, sounds good to me.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Now, the next part of the form deals with qualifications. Do you have the water safety certificate? We absolutely insist on that.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Yes, I do.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: So how long will it last before you have to do a refresher course?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: I took it last November so it'll run out in October. Q5

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay, good. Now, what about work experience as a lifeguard?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Well, I've had about four months experience.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Which swimming pool was that at? I need to have details if your employer obviously so we can get a reference.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Oh, it was at the beach here in Fernley. I can get the number of the person you need to contact. Q6

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Good. And do you have any other additional skills I can put down?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: You can put down diving. I've done that for a long time now. Q7

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: I'm also keen on rock climbing but that's not really relevant here.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: No, okay. And I need to ask when you would prefer to work. You can choose either Saturday mornings or any time Monday to Friday. Q8

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: We've got enough people on Sundays at the moment.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: Well, not Monday to Friday because I'm at the restaurant weekday evenings.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay. We open at 6. Could you start that early?

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: No, that's fine. I'd prefer that to working late.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Okay. Now I need to speak to the committee who run the sports center here.

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: But you should hear back from us pretty soon and then they'll probably arrange an interview.

cues.speaker: STAFF
cues.text: Thanks very much. Great. Now, before you go, I'd just like to ask you how you found out about our advertisement. We always ask this. Was it from the newspaper or the radio? I heard the advertisement this morning when I was driving into college. I don't usually read the local paper. Q10

cues.speaker: PETER
cues.text: All right. Thanks. Well, that's all. Hope to see you soon.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: on how to become a self-made millionaire.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Everybody dreams of becoming a millionaire one day. So we asked Arthur Knowles, who made his millions in the plumbing business

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: to give the budding entrepreneurs among you a few tips on how to make your first million. Arthur, welcome to the program. Thanks, Sue. So, Arthur, what advice do you have for our listeners?

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Well, one thing I've heard people say is that when you're starting up a business,

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: you can't afford to make mistakes.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Well, I believe in the old saying a person who never made a mistake, never made anything. Q11

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: You can't really predict when you'll make mistakes and you have to look at them as a positive experience

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: and one that means you won't make the same mistake again.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: You need to be able to cope with the world of business.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: But according to recent American business school studies, believing in yourself isn't enough by itself to guarantee success.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Confidence can be a good thing, but a person can have too much confidence. Q12

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: And people who try to learn to be confident by buying those how to succeed books are just wasting their time.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: The advice given in these American studies was that being a successful entrepreneur comes down to having the right attitude.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: It's no good getting depressed every time something goes wrong.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Always keep your goals in mind and never give up. Q13

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: And don't listen to all the people around you who say, oh, this will never work.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: One thing I've learned in business is that you don't have to be an expert in everything, like marketing, for example. Q14

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: When I started my business, I tried to do it all myself.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: But I soon realized that although I knew everything there was to know about plumbing, I didn't have much idea about how to sell my ideas.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: So I got someone who knew more about this to take care of the marketing side of things for me.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Then as for leadership, well, you've got to be someone your workers look up to because you've been seen to make the right decisions. Q15

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: You have to be able to control people, but listen to them at the same time.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Some people are driven to make their companies successful, but that too often leads to a ruthless approach.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Then there's the question of taking risks, even calculated ones.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: I personally feel it's actually better to tread carefully when it comes to taking short-term risks. Q16

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: You need a degree of vision certainly, but it's easy to get carried away by your desire to increase profits.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: And if things go wrong, you can end up losing more than you gain.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: So if you have a great idea for a business, what should you do next?

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Well, the first thing to ask yourself is whether there's a need for your product or service. Q17

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Can you cater for people's needs better than existing companies?

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: You don't need to worry about whether it's original or not because there isn't always enough of a demand for completely new ideas. Q19

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: And the second thing to ask yourself is not what color should the packet be or how much should it cost, Q20

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: but do I care enough about this idea to dedicate the next 10 years of my life to it? Q18

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: Because realistically, that's how long it will take. Tell us how you got started, Arthur. How do you explain your early success? Well, I started my business just as the economy was going into a recession, which wasn't the best time.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: And I was lucky to survive, especially as the banks weren't being particularly supportive to small businesses at that time.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: If I'd listened to the business advice I was given back then, I'd never have got started. My strengths were that I knew I could provide a better service than my competitors, who really hadn't spotted the opportunities that were out there.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: And that my wife had a good job and was able to pay the household bills while I was getting the company on its feet.

cues.speaker: ARTHUR
cues.text: The first couple of years were very tough, but I knew I would make it eventually.

cues.speaker: SUE
cues.text: Okay, now we're going to take some calls from listeners.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: So Gina, we've got to give our tutors some feedback on how we feel about the course now we've come to the end of our second year.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Is it okay with you if we have a chat together before we go and see him?

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Sure, Charlie.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: So did you choose this university to do performance arts because it's got such a good reputation? Q27

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: That's what hooked me in.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Well, there are other good places which I also considered, but when I looked into things further, I was impressed by the connections this course has with a whole range of theatres of different types. Q21

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: So even though I was tempted to go and study abroad, I decided to come here in the end.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: And you don't regret it? No, it's been brilliant, especially the options this year.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: The body and dance option I did for this term has been particularly stimulating.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I'm sorry I didn't go for that one too, but I did dance and drama, which was brilliant too.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I think the most valuable option I've done was the movement analysis course we did in the first year. Q22

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Absolutely. It's provided a great foundation for all our other works since then.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: So let's talk about our work experience last summer.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: You went to Finland, didn't you?

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: That's right. I was at their National Ballet Theatre.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I didn't get the chance to go on stage, but I helped out with sewing clothes for current productions and even with designing some for future shows. Q23

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: It was brilliant. I got to know a lot of students studying at the local dance school and I may get the chance to go back there next summer.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I've been offered more work at the place where I was working in Canada. Great. So what do you think you gained most from the experience?

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I think I've got much better at controlling my stress levels.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: For me, it was probably the fact that I learned a lot about collaborating with others rather than working independently. Q24

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I was lucky to be able to do that in a situation that wasn't too stressful.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Also, I had to organise my time well, but I've always been reasonably good at that.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: That's good. So we've got quite a few things ready to say to our tutor.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: It would be a good chance to ask him any questions we have to, of course.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I also think it could be helpful to discuss our future plans.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: For example, what we're planning to do are dissertations on.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Sure. I was unsure about whether to focus on globalisation in dance or on stage design.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I did an essay on globalisation in my first year and really enjoyed it.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: But then I saw a spectacular production at the Royal Opera House, and that settled me on stage design. Q25

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I know another student who's planning to work on that too, so we can discuss things together a bit.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Okay. That could be useful.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I'm planning to do something on current trends and contemporary dance for my dissertation.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: That sounds pretty challenging. It's a big topic.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: It might not be easy to organise in a coherent way.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I've thought about it quite a lot, and I think that'll be okay, and I feel confident about how to write a longer piece of work.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I'm in a bit of a panic, though, about how I'll get through all the literature. Q26

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: There seems to be so much. Hopefully it won't all be relevant.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Quite.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: So have you made any career plans yet?

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I'm still undecided. I've thought about performance, of course.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Yes, I think lots of graduates from here take that route, but it's a hard life involving lots of tough repetitive practice,

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: as well as actually appearing on stage.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Yes, but the performance I've met know that's essential for the job, and say they wouldn't change what they do for the world.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I know lots of graduates go into education, teaching at various levels, but that means doing some kind of post-grad certificate. Q28

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: But I think it would be interesting, rewarding work.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: I was wondering about theatre management as a possible option. Q29

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: That's what our tutor did before he got into teaching, isn't it?

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Yes, but he said he quickly realised it wasn't for him. He wasn't earning enough to live on.

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: I can imagine his communication skills are better than his business skills as well.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: Marketing's a possibility, of course. Q30

cues.speaker: CHARLIE
cues.text: Sure. I've read something saying it can be an interesting career, though I don't think many graduates go for this.

cues.speaker: GINA
cues.text: But that might mean there's not so much competition as in many other fields of dance. Right. So now should we make a list?

cues.speaker: LECTURER
cues.text: Hello everybody. I'm here today to tell you about a new research study that my team here at the University is doing on the sea lions that live along the coast of Western Australia. You may be wondering why we've been studying this animal. Well, Australian sea lions have been identified as an endangered species. So there's a real need to count them and find out just how many there are. Up until 1892 the population of these animals was severely depleted because of hunting. That's no longer allowed. But today there is a new danger. Sea lions often forage for food in the same areas along the coastlines where there are nets used to catch sharks. Unfortunately, they tend to get caught up in the nets by accident and drown. Now we wanted to monitor the population of sea lions in this area, but we weren't sure of the best way to do it. There are several different animal tracking methods which vary in their effectiveness and there are different factors to consider. One of the most important of these is the cost. But you also have to consider how easy your chosen method is to use. You may choose a traditional method like a plastic tag. They're relatively straightforward to attach, but they're really only suitable to use with animals that you can catch quite easily. You might also go with a more modern method like GPS tracking, which uses satellite technology to transmit data on the animal around the clock. One drawback for marine animals though is that they don't transmit a signal in the ocean. You only get data when they're on land. There are certain large animals in remote areas that have to be tracked using a helicopter. The polar bear is a good example. Now, an important part of tracking is being able to clearly identify the animal. Some, like zebras, are identified by markings such as their stripes. While the dolphin usually has distinguishing scars on its body that can help tell them apart. Sea lions don't have any markings like this, which is just one of the challenges of tracking them. When researchers in Perth tried to use electronic tags in a sea lion study, they found that the sea lions had removed their tracking devices by deliberately rubbing up against rocks. This was something the researchers hadn't anticipated. Researchers in California studying American sea lions tried a different method. They applied paint to the animals. They thought this would be a better, less invasive means of identification. Unfortunately, this didn't work so well either because sea lions molt every year and shed their fur along with the identifying mark. So let's look at our current study. We have several aims that we'd like to achieve. The first of these is to try to establish where the sea lions can be identified from the whiskers on their face. These are much coarser than a cat's whiskers so easier to see. Our theory is that the pattern of these whiskers may be as individual as a fingerprint on a human. If this is in fact true, then we think this could be an effective way to identify them. Our second aim is to come up with a diagram of sea lion whisker patterns, so this can be used as a guide for us and other studies. We're using a few different methods to help us do all this. We know that we need to build up a wide range of visual data. So firstly, we've been in touch with zoos around Australia to gather photographs from them or the faces of any sea lions they have. This won't be enough to achieve our purpose though, so we're also broadening our search by inviting the public to take part in our research. We're hoping this will result in hundreds of useful images we can use. You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the listening answer sheet. You have two minutes left. You have one minute left. Please stop writing and wait for your question booklet to be collected. Q31
